To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we can tell people apart and tell them together.

1) the ability to tell people together is an essential component of voice-identity recognition; 2) listeners can overcome substantial within-person variability in vocal signals to obtain a stable perception of person identity; and 3) listeners are more likely to do so when the variability is systematic and predictable.
listeners can generalize voice-identity information from variable vocal signals, and this generalization is affected by the amount of variability in the vocal stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how people perceive and recognize each other from their voices, and how we can best understand this process.
how listeners perceive and process the variable vocal signals that we encounter in everyday life.
understanding how listeners can generalize across the highly variable vocal signals of the same speaker.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we need to study the effects of variability, not just the effects of variability.
the human voice is a flexible and dynamic signal that can be perceived as an individual identity across different vocal contexts.
“flexibility is the key to success in voice perception”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human vocal system is highly flexible and that we need to take this into account when studying voice perception and voice identity processing.
the voice is a flexible signal and that we need to understand how listeners can use the information in this signal to recognize the identity of the talker.
the voice is a flexible instrument, which allows us to express a variety of social and emotional meanings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of voice-identity perception needs to be broadened to account for both within-person and between-person variability, in addition to their interaction.
the ability to tell people together is a fundamental component of voice-identity perception and is an essential feature of the human communication system.
listeners are sensitive to within-person variability in voices, and that this variability is not a random noise that obscures voice-identity processing.
